description: How designers use prototypes, ergonomics, anthropometrics and user feedback to improve products iteratively.
content_html:
Why Designers Build Prototypes

A prototype is a test vehicle. Designers build prototypes not because they expect them to be perfect, but because physical and digital models reveal problems that drawings and calculations cannot. When a design exists only as a sketch or a CAD file, it is possible to miss details that become immediately obvious the moment someone holds or interacts with the product.

Prototypes range widely in fidelity. A low-fidelity prototype might be a rough card model made in an afternoon to check the proportions of a product or whether a handle fits a hand. A high-fidelity prototype is a near-production unit used in the final stages of testing — made from the correct materials, with working mechanisms, and used to gather final approval before tooling for manufacture. Both types serve a purpose; choosing the wrong fidelity wastes time and money.

Key Fact

Prototypes range from low-fidelity (rough models to test form or scale) to high-fidelity (near-production models to test function and finish). Lower fidelity is used earlier in the process when many ideas are still in play; higher fidelity is used later when a design is being finalised.

What Prototypes Are Used to Test

A well-designed test programme evaluates a prototype against the criteria in the design specification. Typical tests cover:

  • Fitness for purpose — does the product do what the brief requires? A waterproof case that lets water in after 30 minutes is not fit for purpose regardless of its appearance.
  • Functionality — do all mechanisms, controls, and components work correctly together? A folding mechanism that catches and jams fails a functionality test even if each individual part is dimensionally correct.
  • Marketability — does the product appeal to the intended user? User panels may assess aesthetic appeal, perceived quality, and willingness to purchase.
  • Safety — does the product meet relevant safety standards? Products for children must be tested against requirements such as choking-hazard rules (no component smaller than 45 mm in any direction for products intended for children under 3).

Ergonomics

Ergonomics is the science of making products fit people rather than expecting people to adapt to products. An ergonomically designed tool is shaped to match the natural movements of the human hand, wrist, and arm, reducing the force required and the risk of repetitive strain. Ergonomics considers not just physical dimensions but also cognitive factors: a control panel with too many buttons, inconsistently labelled, creates cognitive overload and is ergonomically poor even if it is physically comfortable to touch.

When testing ergonomics, designers observe users interacting with a prototype in realistic conditions. A torque wrench that is comfortable to hold during light use may cause wrist fatigue after 30 minutes of heavy use — only testing under realistic conditions reveals this.

Anthropometrics

Anthropometrics is the collection and use of human body measurement data. Designers use percentile tables to design for the range of users they expect to encounter. A product designed for the 50th percentile fits the average user but excludes half the population at each extreme. Designing for the 5th to 95th percentile range is standard practice — this ensures the product works for 90% of the expected user population.

Common anthropometric measurements used in product design include hand grip span, finger length, shoulder width, eye height (standing and seated), reach distance, and foot length. Seat heights, door handle positions, keyboard dimensions, and steering wheel diameters are all derived from anthropometric data.

Key Fact

Designing for the 5th to 95th percentile means the product works for 90% of the expected user population. Designing only for the average (50th percentile) user excludes 50% of users at the taller, shorter, larger, or smaller extremes of the population range.

Testing and Feedback

User testing generates feedback that designers use to make informed decisions about changes. Effective user testing uses structured methods: task-based testing (asking a user to perform a specific action and observing where they struggle), think-aloud protocols (asking the user to describe what they are thinking while using the prototype), and rating scales (asking users to score specific attributes such as comfort, clarity, and visual appeal).

Examiners expect students to understand that feedback from user testing informs design decisions throughout the process, not just at the final stage. A designer who tests only a finished prototype and then modifies it is doing less effective design than one who tests a low-fidelity model early, identifies a structural problem, and revises the specification before any expensive materials are committed.

Iterative design follows a cycle: build → test → evaluate findings → modify → build again. Each cycle produces a design that is better informed than the previous version. The cycle continues until the product meets all specification criteria or until time and budget constraints require a decision to proceed with the best available version.

The key distinction examiners look for is whether feedback genuinely informs decisions or merely documents what happened. A strong response identifies a specific finding from testing (e.g. “users with small hands found the grip diameter of 45 mm caused fatigue after 10 minutes”), the decision it triggered (“the grip diameter was reduced to 32 mm and a softer thermoplastic elastomer grip was added”), and how the next test confirmed the change worked. Feedback that does not change anything is not iterative design — it is observation.

Critical Analysis and Evaluation

Critical analysis of a design means systematically assessing how well it meets each specification criterion, identifying where it falls short, and explaining what evidence supports that judgement. Examiners reward evaluations that are specific and evidence-based. “The handle was comfortable” is not an evaluation; “seven out of eight test users rated handle comfort above 4 out of 5, but the one user with smaller hands rated it 2, suggesting the lower grip limit should be reduced” is an evaluation.

Good evaluation also considers fitness for purpose holistically — a product may pass every individual specification test but still fail to feel right in use, because real use reveals interactions between criteria that individual tests do not capture.

Examiners have identified a recurring error: students describe user testing as useful only because it “improves the final product.” This misses half the mark. The examiner-rewarded point is that feedback from user testing informs design decisions throughout the iterative process — changing the specification, modifying the approach, and redirecting resources before expensive commitments are made. A response that shows testing changing an early prototype specification is stronger than one that shows testing polishing a nearly-finished product.
exam_tip_html: For prototyping questions, always explain what is being tested, how it is tested, and what decision the result informs. For anthropometrics questions, state the percentile range being designed for (5th to 95th is the standard) and explain why, rather than just using the term. For evaluation questions, avoid vague claims (‘the product was comfortable’) and use evidence-based language (‘six out of eight users rated grip comfort 4–5 out of 5’). Examiners explicitly reward feedback that informs decisions throughout the process, not just at the end.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Prototypes range from low-fidelity (cheap, quick, early-stage form tests) to high-fidelity (near-production models for final approval). The right fidelity depends on what is being tested and how much the design has developed.
  • Ergonomics matches products to human physical and cognitive capabilities; anthropometrics provides the body measurement data (typically 5th to 95th percentile) that makes ergonomic design measurable.
  • Iterative design uses each test cycle’s findings to inform the next design decision — not just to improve the final product, but to redirect resources and revise specifications throughout the process.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes a low-fidelity prototype?
A) A near-production model made from the correct materials used in final approval testing
B) A rough model made quickly from card or foam to test the form or scale of a product
C) A computer simulation that predicts stress distribution under load
D) A digital animation of the final product for client presentation
practice_questions.marks: B) A rough model made quickly from card or foam to test the form or scale of a product [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term 'ergonomics' in product design.
practice_questions.marks: Ergonomics is the science of designing products to fit the physical and cognitive abilities of users (1 mark), minimising discomfort, fatigue, and error during use (1 mark). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how a designer would use anthropometric data when designing the seat height of a children's chair for primary school classrooms.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks. Identifies the relevant body measurement: seated popliteal height (distance from the floor to the back of the bent knee) for the target age range (1 mark); explains percentile application: uses 5th to 95th percentile data to ensure the chair height works for 90% of the target user group (1 mark); explains the practical outcome: sets a seat height range that allows feet to rest flat on the floor without the seat edge cutting into the thigh, supporting circulation and posture (1 mark). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why it is important for designers to use iterative testing throughout the design process rather than only testing the final prototype.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Early testing reveals structural or ergonomic problems when changes are cheap (1 mark); testing a low-fidelity prototype can identify a specification error before expensive materials are committed (1 mark); feedback at each stage informs subsequent design decisions, not just product polish (1 mark); a design error discovered only at the final prototype stage may require the entire design to be reworked, whereas the same error found early may be resolved by a minor specification change (1 mark). [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: A designer is developing a new electric power drill for professional tradespeople. Evaluate how the designer could use user testing to assess and improve the ergonomics of the drill's handle.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Evaluates the testing process at multiple stages. Initial low-fidelity handle tests using foam models allow a range of grip spans and diameters to be assessed quickly; anthropometric data (5th to 95th percentile grip span for adult workers) informs the starting dimensions. Structured user testing with professional tradespeople involves task-based tests under realistic loads and durations, revealing fatigue onset and pain points that brief handling cannot detect. Think-aloud protocol captures cognitive ergonomics: unclear trigger mechanisms or awkward mode-switching positions are identified. Rating scales quantify comfort, control, and perceived safety. Findings inform iterative specification changes: reducing handle diameter, adding grip zones, adjusting trigger force. Final high-fidelity prototype confirms changes work before production tooling. Strong evaluation acknowledges limitations: user testing a small panel may not capture all hand sizes or use cases across the professional trades. Secure: Testing process described at two or more stages with clear link to improvement. Developing: Testing described but links to specific ergonomic decisions are weak. Emerging: General description of user testing only. [10 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what designers mean by 'fitness for purpose' and describe two tests a designer might carry out to evaluate whether a children's waterproof lunchbox meets this criterion.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 6 marks. Fitness for purpose definition: the product successfully fulfils the requirements of the design brief and meets all criteria in the design specification (1 mark); for this product, this means the lunchbox keeps food contained, remains waterproof, is safe for children to use, and withstands everyday handling (1 mark). Test 1: water immersion test — submerge the lunchbox in water for a specified period (e.g. 10 minutes) and check for moisture ingress inside; this directly tests the waterproof seal performance against a measurable specification point (1 mark + application 1 mark). Test 2: drop test — drop the lunchbox from a height representing a typical child dropping it (e.g. 1 m onto a hard floor) and inspect the seal, hinges and body for damage; this tests whether the product survives realistic handling conditions (1 mark + application 1 mark). [6 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Designing a product handle for the 5th to 95th percentile means the product will be suitable for approximately what proportion of the expected user population?
Which of the following is the best example of ergonomic design?
options: A kitchen knife with a bright red handle
A handle shaped to reduce wrist rotation and grip force during use
A product made from a recycled polymer
A product with a high-gloss surface finish

knowledge_checks.q: A _____ prototype is a rough model built from card or foam to test the form or scale of a product at an early stage.
_____ is the study of human body measurements used to inform the size and proportions of products designed for human use.
Match each testing term to its correct description:
right: Whether a product meets all criteria in the design specification and brief
Designing products to fit the physical and cognitive abilities of users
Using human body measurement data to set product dimensions

flashcard_questions.q: What is a prototype in product design?
flashcard_questions.a: An early physical or digital model built to test aspects of a design before full production.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between low-fidelity and high-fidelity prototypes?
flashcard_questions.a: Low-fidelity is rough (card, foam) for early form testing; high-fidelity is near-production quality for final approval.
The product successfully fulfils the design brief and meets all criteria in the specification.
The science of designing products to fit human physical and cognitive abilities, reducing fatigue and error.
The study of human body measurements used to inform product dimensions and proportions.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is designing for the 5th to 95th percentile better than designing for the 50th percentile?
flashcard_questions.a: It accommodates 90% of users; the 50th percentile alone excludes half the population at size extremes.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of an anthropometric measurement used in product design.
flashcard_questions.a: Hand grip span — used to set handle diameters for tools and equipment.

flashcard_questions.q: Why should user testing happen throughout the design process, not only at the end?
flashcard_questions.a: Early testing finds problems when changes are cheap; late testing only improves a nearly-finished product.
A cycle of building, testing, evaluating findings, and modifying — repeated until the specification is met.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a think-aloud protocol used for in user testing?
flashcard_questions.a: Asking users to describe their thinking while using a prototype, revealing confusion or difficulty.

glossary_terms.definition: An early physical or digital model of a product built to test one or more aspects of its design before full production, ranging from rough foam models to fully functional pre-production units.
The science of designing products and environments to fit the physical and cognitive abilities of the people who use them, minimising discomfort, fatigue, and error.
The study of human body measurements, such as height, reach, grip span, and seated dimensions, used to inform the size and proportions of products designed for human use.
Whether a product successfully fulfils the requirements of the design brief and meets all criteria in the design specification.
